title: A Pattern Language — curated Containers Hamlet catalogue
attribution: Pattern numbers and titles are referenced from Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa and Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel, A Pattern Language (Oxford University Press, 1977). Summaries and hamlet interpretations here are original text, not quotations.
copyrightNote: The source book is copyrighted. This catalogue references pattern numbers and titles, links to the source, and uses new summaries and interpretations. It does not reproduce the book text or illustrations.

verification.method: Pattern numbers and titles checked against the contents and summary pages of the 1977 edition PDF.
verification.scope: Title/number mapping only. Interpretations are original design notes, not claims about the authors’ intent.

patterns.title: Degrees of Publicness
patterns.summary: Make the change from public arrival to shared, semi-private and private places gradual and legible.
patterns.problem: A single hard edge between public and private makes community life either exposed or inaccessible.
patterns.proposal: Use a sequence of thresholds, shared edges and clearly private territory rather than one binary boundary.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The lane, forecourt, shared paths, lodge terrace, home porches and door thresholds should form a readable gradient. Not every route should pass directly beside a bedroom window.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline has an entrance, shared lanes and trails, private homes and porches, but the transitions are not consistently modelled, named or evaluated.
patterns.alternatives: Compare the dispersed baseline with the central clearing and woodland-spine scenarios, especially where shared paths meet private porches.
patterns.tradeoffs: More thresholds can make a place feel welcoming or over-controlled. Signs, gates and lighting can clarify or exclude.
patterns.unresolved: No observational evidence of how residents, visitors or service people actually experience the edges.
evaluationQuestions: Can a visitor tell which places are public, shared, semi-private and private?
Can a resident reach a shared facility without crossing a private room or window?
Are thresholds usable in snow, rain and low light?
patterns.relationshipNote: Publicness depends on the cluster, the small gathering place and the entrance transition; those patterns make the gradient physical.

patterns.title: House Cluster
patterns.summary: Arrange a small number of dwellings so they form a recognisable neighbourhood while retaining private territory.
patterns.problem: Scattered homes can miss casual neighbourliness; too much clustering can erase privacy.
patterns.proposal: Group homes around a shared edge or outdoor place at a scale where residents can recognise one another.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The six homes can remain dispersed but should be evaluated as clusters around shared paths, a glade or a service point. The lodge is not a substitute for neighbourliness.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline disperses six homes across the site and places the lodge near the entrance. The current arrangement has no formal cluster evaluation.
patterns.alternatives: Test Scenario B (central clearing) and Scenario C (woodland spine with social pockets) against the baseline.
patterns.tradeoffs: Clustering shortens some infrastructure and increases casual contact, but can reduce visual privacy and concentrate disturbance.
patterns.unresolved: No resident preference data or measured walking distances for the alternatives.
evaluationQuestions: Can residents recognise a small cluster without a gate or private road?
Does each home retain a private edge?
Are shared facilities reachable from more than one cluster?
patterns.relationshipNote: A cluster needs common land and a legible publicness gradient to avoid becoming either a private compound or an unprotected shared yard.

patterns.title: Small Public Squares
patterns.summary: Provide small, enclosed outdoor gathering places at the scale of everyday encounters.
patterns.problem: One large central space may be too formal or too far away for casual use.
patterns.proposal: Create several modest outdoor places where a few people can pause, talk or wait.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: A widened path, a rock glade or a lodge forecourt can serve this role. A formal urban square is not assumed to be appropriate in the woodland.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline has informal outdoor areas and a lodge porch, but no dedicated small gathering place.
patterns.alternatives: The woodland-spine scenario can add two or three small pockets rather than one central square.
patterns.tradeoffs: More small places spread maintenance and may fragment activity. One central place is easier to service but less private.
patterns.unresolved: No assessment of sun, wind, snow clearing, seating or acoustic comfort at candidate places.
evaluationQuestions: Is there a small place to pause within a short walk of each home?
Does it have a sense of enclosure without becoming a trap?
Is it usable in winter and by people with reduced mobility?
patterns.relationshipNote: A small square works when it is part of the publicness sequence and on a path with a real destination.

patterns.title: Common Land
patterns.summary: Set aside shared land that residents collectively use and care for, distinct from private lots and public park.
patterns.problem: Without explicit common land, shared outdoor life becomes accidental or privately claimed.
patterns.proposal: Define common land with clear use, access and stewardship, and connect it to the homes it serves.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The community land trust should identify the glade, shoreline buffers, woodland and lodge grounds as shared land with different rules; not all land is equally public.
patterns.currentResponse: The fiction includes shared landscape and a community land trust, but ownership, access and stewardship are not mapped consistently.
patterns.alternatives: Scenario B gives a central common clearing; Scenario C uses a linear spine of smaller common pockets.
patterns.tradeoffs: More common land can support shared life but increases maintenance and may disturb habitat. Protected land may need to remain inaccessible.
patterns.unresolved: No legal survey, stewardship agreement or ecological assessment.
evaluationQuestions: Which land is commonly held, which is private and which is protected?
Who maintains each shared place?
Does shared use damage sensitive habitat?
patterns.relationshipNote: Common land needs site repair and positive outdoor space so shared use does not become an excuse to develop sensitive ground.

patterns.title: Public Outdoor Room
patterns.summary: Make a sheltered outdoor place that feels like a room and supports informal gathering.
patterns.problem: Outdoor shared space without enclosure, shelter or a reason to stay becomes circulation space.
patterns.proposal: Use a roof, wall, screen, level change or planting to create a defined outdoor room with seating and a view.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The lodge porch and a sheltered picnic/workshop edge could be public outdoor rooms. The six cabin porches are more private and should not be treated as the same social space.
patterns.currentResponse: The lodge has a covered porch; individual homes have porches. Their social role and weather protection are not evaluated.
patterns.alternatives: Test a sheltered shared terrace between the lodge and the path, or a small covered pocket on the spine.
patterns.tradeoffs: A generous shared room supports events but can create noise and reduce privacy for nearby homes.
patterns.unresolved: No acoustic, wind, snow or furniture study.
evaluationQuestions: Does the place have a clear edge and a reason to linger?
Can it be used by one person without booking an event?
Is it sheltered from wind, rain and snow?
patterns.relationshipNote: A public outdoor room is a shared version of the private outdoor room and should sit near common areas, not on a private porch.

patterns.title: Site Repair
patterns.summary: Place buildings and infrastructure where they avoid unnecessary damage and help repair already disturbed ground.
patterns.problem: Convenient building sites can destroy the most valuable vegetation, drainage or habitat.
patterns.proposal: Read the land first, use already disturbed areas where possible, and restore the damage that construction causes.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Test each home, path and service corridor against rock, wetland, drainage, tree roots and habitat. A buffer on a drawing is not proof that damage is avoided.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline has illustrative buffers, rock and wetland constraints, and elevated foundations, but no survey or construction-impact assessment.
patterns.alternatives: The scenario comparison should show which footprints and paths move into or out of sensitive areas.
patterns.tradeoffs: A compact cluster may shorten services but concentrate damage; a dispersed layout may protect one glade while fragmenting habitat elsewhere.
patterns.unresolved: No ecological survey, arborist assessment, drainage model or construction-access plan.
evaluationQuestions: Is this footprint on already disturbed ground?
What vegetation, drainage or habitat is affected?
Can the damage be restored, and who is responsible?
patterns.relationshipNote: Site repair constrains the house cluster, common land and paths; those patterns should follow the land rather than force a geometry.

patterns.title: South Facing Outdoors
patterns.summary: Put the main outdoor places on the sunny side and use the building to shelter them from wind.
patterns.problem: A porch or garden on the cold, shaded side will be used less, even if it has a good view.
patterns.proposal: Orient the principal outdoor room toward winter sun and provide wind shelter without blocking summer shade.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Check porch orientation, roof overhangs and snow shedding. A lake view may justify a west or north porch, but the trade-off must be explicit.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline orients homes to views and access; porch orientation is not systematically evaluated for winter sun.
patterns.alternatives: A scenario-level solar/wind study could test whether the lodge terrace and cabin porches have a usable winter microclimate.
patterns.tradeoffs: South glazing and porches gain sun but can overheat, lose heat and reduce privacy. A view orientation may outweigh solar gain.
patterns.unresolved: No solar, wind or snowdrift model; no measured microclimate.
evaluationQuestions: Which outdoor places receive useful winter sun?
Are they sheltered from prevailing wind and snow?
Does the orientation trade a view for comfort?
limitations: No site-specific solar or wind study
patterns.relationshipNote: South-facing outdoor space and positive outdoor space reinforce one another; light on two sides affects the interior side of the same decision.

patterns.title: Positive Outdoor Space
patterns.summary: Shape outdoor space with buildings, walls, levels or planting so it has a clear form rather than being leftover gap.
patterns.problem: Space left between buildings often feels like a passage or a residual strip, not a place.
patterns.proposal: Design the outdoor space first, then place the building edges that enclose it.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Evaluate the lodge forecourt, the space between paired homes, the courtyard and the woodland gaps as rooms with clear edges and uses.
patterns.currentResponse: The Courtyard Residence has an explicit courtyard; other homes have porches and decks. Site-wide outdoor space is not evaluated as positive or residual.
patterns.alternatives: Scenario B makes a central outdoor room; Scenario C makes a sequence of smaller pockets.
patterns.tradeoffs: Strong enclosure improves comfort but can block views, light, drainage or wildlife movement.
patterns.unresolved: No spatial-quality or use observation; no wind/sun study.
evaluationQuestions: Does the space have a clear edge and a use?
Is it more than leftover space between buildings?
Does enclosure harm access, daylight or ecology?
patterns.relationshipNote: Positive outdoor space gives the house cluster and common land their physical shape; the outdoor room is its smaller, sheltered version.

patterns.title: Entrance Transition
patterns.summary: Make arrival gradual: path, gate, porch and threshold should give people time and shelter to shift from public to private.
patterns.problem: A door directly on a shared route gives no place to pause, no weather protection and no privacy.
patterns.proposal: Use a sequence of transitional spaces and a visible, sheltered threshold.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Each home needs a legible, step-free arrival sequence with room for a visitor, deliveries, snow and wet clothing. The accessible homes need the threshold detail to work.
patterns.currentResponse: Homes have porches and step-free entrance intent, but threshold dimensions, door clearances, visitor space and winter maintenance are not fully modelled.
patterns.alternatives: Test a deeper covered entry or a small entrance hall in the two accessible homes.
patterns.tradeoffs: A generous transition improves comfort and privacy but consumes floor area and may add heat loss.
patterns.unresolved: No door/threshold construction detail, no snow or drainage detail.
evaluationQuestions: Can a visitor pause out of the weather before entering?
Is the route step-free and clear of snow storage?
Can residents reach the door without passing a private window?
patterns.relationshipNote: The entrance transition is where the publicness gradient becomes a physical threshold; it depends on the path and outdoor space.

patterns.title: Arcades
patterns.summary: A covered walk or gallery can connect entrances and outdoor rooms while giving shelter and a social edge.
patterns.problem: In cold, wet or snowy conditions, an exposed path can make shared life optional in theory but difficult in practice.
patterns.proposal: Use a roofed or screened edge to connect destinations without making every route an interior corridor.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Consider a covered link at the lodge or between a home and a shared workshop, not a continuous enclosed mall. Snow, ice, drainage and maintenance matter.
patterns.currentResponse: The baseline has porches but no shared arcade. The cold-climate idea is not tested.
patterns.alternatives: Test a short covered link at the lodge entrance and a sheltered waiting place on the spine.
patterns.tradeoffs: Cover improves winter use but adds structure, snow load, shading, maintenance and cost; it can also create dark or unsafe edges.
patterns.unresolved: No snow-load, drainage, daylight or maintenance assessment.
evaluationQuestions: Which shared destinations need weather protection?
Can the route be kept clear of snow and ice?
Does the cover create a dark or unsafe place?
patterns.relationshipNote: An arcade is a path with a roof and a social edge; it should not substitute for a good outdoor room or a clear entrance transition.

patterns.title: Paths and Goals
patterns.summary: Connect meaningful destinations with paths shaped by the places they pass, not just the shortest line.
patterns.problem: Paths without destinations become maintenance liabilities; paths that ignore terrain become inaccessible or destructive.
patterns.proposal: Start from destinations and daily activities, then shape the route around land, views, shelter and accessibility.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Map the lodge, homes, workshop, parking, drop-off and shared outdoor places. Distinguish everyday routes from recreational trails and emergency access.
patterns.currentResponse: The site has lanes and trails linking the entrance, homes and lodge, but accessibility, winter maintenance and destination hierarchy are not evaluated.
patterns.alternatives: Scenario C makes the spine explicit; Scenario A relies on dispersed routes; Scenario B shortens some trips but concentrates them.
patterns.tradeoffs: More direct paths reduce walking but may cross sensitive ground or private edges. Longer scenic routes may be pleasant but unsuitable for daily accessibility.
patterns.unresolved: No route-by-route grade, surface, width, lighting or winter assessment.
evaluationQuestions: What everyday destinations does this path connect?
Is it usable by someone with reduced mobility in winter?
Does it cross sensitive land or private space?
patterns.relationshipNote: Paths and goals give the publicness sequence and common land a network; an arcade is a special covered segment, not a replacement for the whole network.

patterns.title: Intimacy Gradient
patterns.summary: Arrange rooms and outdoor spaces from more public to more private, so people can withdraw without crossing private territory.
patterns.problem: A plan that puts the bed beside the front door or makes every room a passage undermines privacy and rest.
patterns.proposal: Place shared living near the entry, then kitchen, then bedrooms and private outdoor places, with a clear route that does not pass through private rooms.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Test the authored accessible interiors and the room-band models for a legible gradient. The long container makes the far end valuable private space.
patterns.currentResponse: Woodland Cottage and Accessible Garden Home have authored room polygons; the other four use provisional bands. The interiors have not been evaluated as a full gradient.
patterns.alternatives: Compare a central-service plan with a linear front-to-back plan in the 40-foot homes.
patterns.tradeoffs: A strong gradient protects privacy but can make the far room feel isolated or make plumbing runs longer.
patterns.unresolved: No acoustic separation, door-swing or occupant-flow analysis.
evaluationQuestions: Can a resident reach a private room without crossing a shared room?
Can a visitor be received without entering the private zone?
Is there a private outdoor place?
patterns.relationshipNote: The intimacy gradient relies on a clear entrance transition and gives meaning to a room of one’s own, alcoves and window places.

patterns.title: Common Areas at the Heart
patterns.summary: Put shared facilities where everyday activity passes and where people can see and reach them, not at a remote edge.
patterns.problem: A common building at the entrance may be convenient for infrastructure but socially peripheral if daily life happens elsewhere.
patterns.proposal: Locate common activities at a crossing of everyday routes and make them visible, accessible and easy to enter for a small purpose.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The lodge is near the entrance. Test whether it is socially central, whether residents pass it on ordinary walks, and whether shared facilities can be used without joining a large event.
patterns.currentResponse: The lodge is a single shared building near the entrance with kitchen, laundry, workshop and gathering space. Its social centrality is asserted, not measured.
patterns.alternatives: A small shared kitchen/workshop pocket on the spine, or a satellite mailbox/tool shed, could complement the lodge.
patterns.tradeoffs: A central lodge supports shared activity but concentrates noise and may dominate the community. Satellite facilities add maintenance but reduce dependence on one building.
patterns.unresolved: No resident activity data, no acoustic or management study.
evaluationQuestions: Does daily life pass the common area?
Can a resident use one facility without joining an event?
Are quiet and noisy activities separated?
patterns.relationshipNote: Common areas need a house cluster and public outdoor room to become a heart; a remote lodge alone cannot create community.

patterns.title: A Room of One’s Own
patterns.summary: Give each resident a private room they can close, personalise and use without negotiating shared space.
patterns.problem: Shared living can leave no place to withdraw, work, rest or host a private conversation.
patterns.proposal: Provide at least one genuinely private room per resident, with a door, daylight and space for their own things.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Check bedroom counts and private space in each home. A one-bedroom home works for one resident or a couple; it is not a universal household model.
patterns.currentResponse: The six homes include one-bedroom and studio arrangements. The accessible homes have one bedroom and no dedicated guest room.
patterns.alternatives: Test a small alcove/workspace within the bedroom or a separate garden studio where site and budget allow.
patterns.tradeoffs: More private rooms increase floor area, cost and energy demand; a small home may need a flexible room instead.
patterns.unresolved: No household composition assumptions or furniture/clearance study.
evaluationQuestions: Does every resident have a door they can close?
Can the room be used for sleep, work or retreat?
Is there daylight and a place for personal belongings?
patterns.relationshipNote: A private room depends on a clear intimacy gradient and is made usable by alcoves and a window place.

patterns.title: Old Age Cottage
patterns.summary: Provide a small, accessible dwelling close to community support so people can remain in the hamlet as they age.
patterns.problem: A remote or stair-only home forces older residents to leave the community when their mobility changes.
patterns.proposal: Include a dwelling that is small, step-free, close to shared facilities and able to accommodate care and visits.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The two accessible homes demonstrate this idea. Test whether they are close enough to the lodge and whether care, deliveries and emergency access work in winter.
patterns.currentResponse: Woodland Cottage and Accessible Garden Home are single-storey accessible demonstrations; the other four are not held to that target.
patterns.alternatives: Assign one accessible home near the lodge or a shared path, or add a guest/carer room to the lodge.
patterns.tradeoffs: A cottage close to the lodge gains support but may lose privacy; a remote cottage gains quiet but makes care harder.
patterns.unresolved: No care model, emergency response time or ageing-in-place review.
evaluationQuestions: Can an older resident reach the lodge without stairs or a car?
Can a carer or visitor reach the door?
Does the home have a private room and a step-free bathroom?
patterns.relationshipNote: An old-age cottage should be part of the common heart and entrance/path network, not an isolated accessible unit at the edge.

patterns.title: Light on Two Sides of Every Room
patterns.summary: Daylight from two directions makes a room feel more balanced and reduces glare compared with a single bright wall.
patterns.problem: A narrow container with windows on only one side can be dark at the back and glaring at the front.
patterns.proposal: Use openings on opposite or adjacent sides, end glazing, clerestories or reflected light where the structure allows.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Test existing rooms for two-sided light. A 2.35 m clear width makes cross-light difficult; end windows, roof lights and open-plan connections may help but add heat loss and structural work.
patterns.currentResponse: The models record openings and orientations, but do not calculate daylight, glare or two-sidedness for every room.
patterns.alternatives: Compare end-window, opposite-window and clerestory strategies in the 40-foot homes.
patterns.tradeoffs: More glazing improves daylight but increases heat loss, solar gain, privacy loss and structural complexity.
patterns.unresolved: No daylight simulation, glare analysis or overheating study.
evaluationQuestions: Does the room receive light from more than one direction?
Is there glare or a dark back wall?
What are the heat-loss and privacy costs?
patterns.relationshipNote: Two-sided light supports south-facing outdoor space and the window place; it can conflict with privacy and heat loss.

patterns.title: Outdoor Room
patterns.summary: Treat a porch, terrace or courtyard as a real room with a floor, shelter, edge and furniture.
patterns.problem: A narrow strip beside a building may be called a porch but cannot support sitting, eating or visiting.
patterns.proposal: Give the outdoor space enough depth, shelter, enclosure and furniture to be used like an indoor room.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Evaluate the six cabin porches and lodge porch for depth, wind, rain, snow, insects, privacy, step-free access and furniture.
patterns.currentResponse: Porches are modelled in the Design Lab; their usability and seasonal performance are not evaluated.
patterns.alternatives: Test a deeper screened porch or a courtyard edge in the accessible homes.
patterns.tradeoffs: A deeper porch improves outdoor living but increases roof area, cost, heat loss and snow load.
patterns.unresolved: No furniture layout, wind-driven rain or snow study.
evaluationQuestions: Can two people sit, eat or talk in the space?
Is it sheltered from rain, wind and snow?
Can it be reached step-free?
patterns.relationshipNote: The outdoor room is the private or shared version of positive outdoor space; it needs sun, shelter and a window/indoor connection.

patterns.title: Tree Places
patterns.summary: Preserve special trees and make places around them for sitting, play or gathering rather than clearing every tree.
patterns.problem: Conventional site clearing removes the trees that give a place its identity and shade.
patterns.proposal: Identify valued trees early, protect their root zones and design paths and outdoor places around them.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The woodland is the hamlet’s character. Map candidate tree places, root protection zones and views; do not treat the whole site as buildable.
patterns.currentResponse: The site has forest, rock and buffers, but no tree survey or root-protection plan. The site plan is illustrative.
patterns.alternatives: Shift a path, porch or parking area to preserve a significant tree; use a tree place as a small shared destination.
patterns.tradeoffs: Preserving trees can constrain foundations, solar access, snow clearing and emergency access; removing them can damage character and habitat.
patterns.unresolved: No arborist survey, root mapping or species/habitat assessment.
evaluationQuestions: Which trees are irreplaceable or culturally important?
Is the root zone protected from construction?
Does the design use the tree as a place, not just an obstacle?
patterns.relationshipNote: Tree places make common land and site repair tangible; a preserved tree can anchor a positive outdoor space or a path destination.

patterns.title: Alcoves
patterns.summary: Small, semi-enclosed nooks let people be together without being on display.
patterns.problem: An open-plan room offers no place for a quiet conversation, a hobby or a person who wants to be nearby but not central.
patterns.proposal: Shape a small recess or partial enclosure with a seat, light and view, connected to a larger room.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Use alcoves for reading, work, a guest bed or a quiet seat in the long container. They must not block the accessible route.
patterns.currentResponse: Not modelled. The interiors have rooms and furniture but no alcove geometry.
patterns.alternatives: Test a window alcove or a shelf-backed seat in the 40-foot homes.
patterns.tradeoffs: Alcoves add enclosure and intimacy but reduce open floor area and can complicate circulation and light.
patterns.unresolved: No furniture, reach-range or route-clearance study.
evaluationQuestions: Is there a place to sit apart without leaving the room?
Does the alcove have light and a view?
Does it obstruct the accessible route?
limitations: Not modelled in the current interiors
patterns.relationshipNote: An alcove supports the intimacy gradient and a room of one’s own at a smaller scale; a window place can be its edge.

patterns.title: Window Place
patterns.summary: Make a comfortable place to sit at a window, with light, a view and a sense of enclosure.
patterns.problem: A window can provide light and view but no usable place to pause, read or watch the weather.
patterns.proposal: Shape a seat, table or alcove at the window with comfortable height, light and a view.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Use window places in the long cabins for reading, work and landscape connection. Include accessible seating and safe window operation; do not block the route.
patterns.currentResponse: Not modelled. Windows are recorded, but no seat or clear floor zone is assigned.
patterns.alternatives: Test a built-in bench with a lift-out accessible seat, or a movable chair for flexibility.
patterns.tradeoffs: Built-ins save space but are hard to change and may not suit all bodies; movable furniture is flexible but can block routes.
patterns.unresolved: No seat height, reach, glare, privacy or window-operation study.
evaluationQuestions: Can a person sit at the window comfortably?
Is the seat accessible and easy to leave?
Is there glare, privacy or overheating?
patterns.relationshipNote: A window place is a small room of one’s own and an alcove at the building edge; it connects the interior to the outdoor room and two-sided light.

extensions.title: Energy patterns developed for Containers Hamlet
extensions.attribution: Original extensions developed for this project. These are not Christopher Alexander patterns and are not attributed to him.
extensions.note: Each extension is a design proposition developed from the residential energy work. The linked Alexander patterns are references to the 1977 book; the extension text is original.

patterns.title: Right-Sized Energy
patterns.summary: Size the electrical system to the life it serves, not to a showroom ideal. A smaller home with a modest load can be better served by a smaller array and battery than a larger home with a larger system.
patterns.problem: Solar arrays and batteries are often sized by ambition, available roof area or a generic package rather than by the number of residents, the season of use and the loads that actually exist.
patterns.proposal: Start from a documented load list and an honest occupancy pattern. Add generation and storage only to meet that demand, including a defined winter reserve. Show the shortfall rather than hiding it in an oversized system.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Woodland Cottage carries 8 panels and a 10 kWh battery for one person and seasonal use; Cross-Stacked Retreat carries 16 panels and 24 kWh for four residents. The difference is justified by occupants and loads, not by floor area alone.
patterns.tradeoffs: A smaller system costs less and uses fewer materials, but it reduces tolerance for cloudy periods and may constrain future needs. A larger system adds embodied impact and maintenance.
patterns.unresolved: No metered consumption exists. The load lists are assumptions, not measurements, and the winter shortfall remains a design problem.
evaluationQuestions: Does the system match the documented load list and occupancy?
Is the winter shortfall visible and planned for?
Could demand reduction replace another panel or battery?

patterns.title: Solar Outdoor Rooms
patterns.summary: A canopy or porch can be both a usable outdoor room and a solar support, provided it does not shade the winter sun the building needs or discharge snow onto a route.
patterns.problem: Solar canopies are often added as equipment, not as architecture. A canopy in the wrong place shades the building, blocks a path or becomes a maintenance problem.
patterns.proposal: Design the canopy as an outdoor room first: shelter, shade, a protected route. Then place panels on it where the winter sun is unobstructed and snow can leave safely.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Courtyard Residence uses a detached east-path canopy; Solar Studio Stack uses a steep winter canopy beside its east path. Neither is placed across the courtyard’s winter sun.
patterns.tradeoffs: A canopy adds structure, wind uplift, snow management and maintenance access. It can improve outdoor use and generation at the same time, or do neither if poorly placed.
patterns.unresolved: Canopy structure, wind uplift, snow shedding and egress are not engineered. The winter shade geometry is simplified.
evaluationQuestions: Does the canopy shelter a real route or outdoor room?
Does it shade the building in winter?
Can snow leave it without crossing an entrance or accessible path?

patterns.title: Shared Energy Infrastructure
patterns.summary: Some electrical services are better shared than duplicated: laundry, water pumping, tools, emergency charging and a larger battery that can support several homes.
patterns.problem: Six independent systems can duplicate expensive equipment and leave each household without a backup. A shared system can also hide dependency and weaken autonomy if it is not governed clearly.
patterns.proposal: Keep essential independent capability in each home, then add a shared layer for high-demand and emergency services. Define metering, governance, maintenance and failure modes before building it.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The common lodge carries a larger shared array, battery and laundry. Each residence keeps its own essential array and battery, and shared electricity is modelled as an option with a stated distribution loss.
patterns.tradeoffs: Sharing reduces duplication and can improve resilience, but adds distribution losses, governance, metering and a single point of failure.
patterns.unresolved: No shared electrical design, protection scheme, metering or cost allocation exists. The microgrid comparison is a conceptual energy balance.
evaluationQuestions: Which services are genuinely better shared?
What happens when the shared system fails?
Is access equitable and is the governance written down?

patterns.title: Winter Resilience
patterns.summary: A home is not winter-resilient because its battery lasts three days. It is resilient when the array can recharge the battery while supplying the load, and when the household has a plan for the days it cannot.
patterns.problem: Average winter generation can look adequate while a five-day cloud sequence, snow cover or a partial array failure leaves the home short.
patterns.proposal: Test consecutive cloudy days, snow-covered arrays, partial failure and loss of shared supply. State the unserved demand and the planned response: reduce load, use shared backup, run a generator or accept the shortfall.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: All six homes show a positive five-day shortfall without shared electricity. The smaller cottage has more days of autonomy but the same structural risk; the larger homes have more generation but larger loads.
patterns.tradeoffs: More battery and more array improve tolerance but add cost and embodied impact. Load reduction and shared backup may be cheaper and more robust.
patterns.unresolved: Weather is synthetic. Snow clearing, battery ageing and cold-weather derating are simplified. No emergency plan is agreed.
evaluationQuestions: What happens on the fifth cloudy day?
Can the array recharge the battery while serving the load?
Is the emergency response written down and practiced?

patterns.title: Essential Electrical Services
patterns.summary: Separate the loads that must continue from the loads that can wait. A small essential circuit can keep communications, ventilation, water, refrigeration and accessibility equipment alive when the whole-house system cannot.
patterns.problem: Treating all loads as equal makes the battery larger and the emergency plan less clear. Treating none as essential leaves people without communications, water or refrigeration.
patterns.proposal: Classify loads as essential continuous, essential intermittent, discretionary, high-demand and accessibility-related. Provide a labelled essential circuit and a reserve that ordinary operation cannot consume.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Each residence records an essential reserve and an essential-load autonomy. The Accessible Garden Home carries a larger reserve for communications and accessibility-related equipment without assuming a specific medical device.
patterns.tradeoffs: A larger essential reserve reduces ordinary autonomy. Omitting a load from the essential list may be unsafe for a particular resident.
patterns.unresolved: Residents have not defined their own essential loads. Accessibility needs vary and must not be assumed.
evaluationQuestions: Which loads must continue, and for how long?
Is the essential circuit labelled and reachable?
Does the reserve reflect the residents’ actual needs?

patterns.title: Repairable Technology
patterns.summary: Choose equipment that can be inspected, isolated, repaired and replaced by a qualified person without dismantling the building.
patterns.problem: Solar, battery and inverter systems are often installed as sealed packages with inaccessible isolators, proprietary parts and no service plan.
patterns.proposal: Keep the service core accessible, label every circuit, use replaceable components and record the maintenance access. Design the array so panels can be reached safely.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Woodland Cottage keeps its array in one reachable row at the eave; the Accessible Garden Home puts four panels on a porch roof that can be inspected from the terrace. Neither treats “install and forget” as a plan.
patterns.tradeoffs: Accessible, repairable equipment can cost more and take more space. Proprietary all-in-one systems may be cheaper but harder to service.
patterns.unresolved: No equipment has been selected. Maintenance access, spare parts and service intervals are not designed.
evaluationQuestions: Can the inverter and battery be isolated without a ladder?
Are the array and canopy serviceable safely?
Are spare parts and a service plan available?

patterns.title: Woodland Preservation
patterns.summary: Treat the woodland as the primary infrastructure. Put buildings, arrays and paths in existing clearings, on roofs and on already-disturbed ground before clearing mature trees.
patterns.problem: A solar calculation can be “improved” by removing trees, quietly trading habitat, shade, privacy and fire resilience for generation.
patterns.proposal: Model the trees as a constraint. Keep arrays on roofs, canopies and existing clearings. Record the shade loss and accept it rather than clearing the woodland.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Offset Stack puts its second array on the ground in the existing east clearing rather than removing trees. The woodland shade is a recorded loss, not a reason to clear.
patterns.tradeoffs: Keeping trees reduces winter generation and can increase snow and leaf maintenance. Removing them changes habitat, privacy, wind and fire behaviour.
patterns.unresolved: The tree model is a simplified cylinder scatter, not a survey. Habitat value and fire behaviour are not assessed.
evaluationQuestions: Could the array move to a roof or existing clearing?
What is the shaded yield, and is it accepted?
Does the design protect the trees that matter most?

patterns.title: Seasonal Adaptation
patterns.summary: Design for several occupancies, not one: summer, shoulder season, intermittent winter and full-time winter. The same home may need different loads, different rooms and a different relationship to the array.
patterns.problem: A cottage sized for summer may be presented as a year-round home, or a full-time home may be modelled only in average conditions.
patterns.proposal: Record separate summer, shoulder, intermittent-winter and unoccupied profiles. Show the consumption, generation and autonomy for each. Let the household choose its pattern honestly.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: Woodland Cottage is sized for summer and intermittent winter, not full-time winter living. Solar Studio Stack is modelled as a full-time single-person home. Their systems differ because their lives differ.
patterns.tradeoffs: A seasonal home uses fewer resources but may not support ageing in place or a change of circumstances. A full-time home needs more winter capacity.
patterns.unresolved: Occupancy is assumed. The water system, access and winterization are not fully designed for every pattern.
evaluationQuestions: Which seasons is the home actually used?
Does the winter profile assume full-time occupation?
What changes if the household stays all winter?

patterns.title: Accessible Service Infrastructure
patterns.summary: Electrical and water controls, battery isolation and maintenance access must be reachable and operable by the people who live there, without climbing and without an unplanned dependence on others.
patterns.problem: Service rooms, inverters and batteries are often placed in basements, lofts or locked cupboards that an accessible route does not reach.
patterns.proposal: Put the service core on an accessible route, at a reachable height, with clear labelling and a safe isolation sequence. Keep canopies and arrays out of the step-free route and design snow to leave away from it.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The Accessible Garden Home keeps its utility cupboard at the entrance, puts four panels on a porch roof inspectable from the terrace, and uses snow guards. It does not claim that the electrical work is accessible to a resident without training.
patterns.tradeoffs: Accessible service space can consume floor area and cost more. Remote monitoring can reduce the need to reach equipment but adds dependency on communications.
patterns.unresolved: Controls have not been tested with disabled residents. Maintenance still requires a qualified electrical contractor.
evaluationQuestions: Can a resident reach the main isolation switch without stairs?
Are controls at a usable height and clearly labelled?
Does solar infrastructure obstruct a step-free route?

patterns.title: Low-Energy Domestic Life
patterns.summary: The cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one not used. Efficient appliances, smaller rooms, shared facilities, daylight, clothes drying and modest hot-water use can avoid panels and batteries entirely.
patterns.problem: Adding generation is more visible than reducing demand, so the array grows while the refrigerator, lighting and standby loads remain inefficient.
patterns.proposal: Reduce demand first: efficient refrigeration, LED lighting, DC-native devices, shared laundry, short showers, passive cooling and daylight. Then size the array and battery for what remains.
patterns.hamletInterpretation: The six homes share a modest construction language and a low-energy appliance set. The shared lodge takes laundry and high-demand equipment out of the individual homes. The comparison shows the equivalent panel count that could be avoided by demand reduction.
patterns.tradeoffs: Reducing demand can mean changing habits, sharing facilities or accepting a smaller appliance. Efficiency improvements have their own embodied impact.
patterns.unresolved: No lifecycle or carbon assessment is claimed. Appliance efficiencies are assumptions, not measured performance.
evaluationQuestions: Which loads could be reduced or shared before adding panels?
Are the appliances the most efficient available?
Does the home make low-energy habits easy?
